A Comparative Life Cycle Cost Analysis of Sustainable 
and Conventional Buildings 
Literature survey 
The Life Cycle Costing (LCC) is widely used economic evaluation method that 
calculates the total cost of a building throughout its entire life span. This includes 
prior construction costs, operational expenditure, maintenance, and disposal costs. 
Research indicates that operational cost is about 60–80% of the total life cycle 
costs, which highlight their importance in cost assessments. 
Sustainable buildings are constructed mainly to minimize environmental impact 
and reduce resource use. But, studies convey that their initial construction costs are 
generally 5–15% higher than those of conventional buildings. 
Despite of expensive prior construction cost, multiple studies determine that 
sustainable buildings are: 
 20–40% Efficient in energy consumption 
 30–50% Efficient in water usage 
 10–25% less maintenance costs 
Over a typical lifespan of 30–50 years, these savings convert into 10–20% of less 
total life cycle costs compared to conventional buildings.

(a) Actions Taken to Seek and Respond to Feedback: 
In order to improve the analytical depth of my literature analysis, I actively sought 
input from peers and my academic supervisor throughout this research. According 
to early comments, my review mostly relied on broad assertions regarding the cost 
disparities between conventional and sustainable buildings, lacking adequate 
quantitative support and Sydney specific data. In response, I used empirical data 
from industry reports (GBCA, 2023) and peer reviewed studies (e.g., Zuo et al., 
2017; Cabeza et al., 2014) to bolster claims that sustainable buildings achieve 10 – 
20% lower overall life cycle costs over 30 –5 0 years and 20 – 40% energy 
savings. 
For instance, I created Table 1 (Literature Summary Table) that displays side by 
side cost components (original cost, energy cost, water cost, maintenance, total

LCC) for sustainable vs. conventional structures in response to input regarding the 
need for more precise comparable measurements. This made it possible for me to 
transition from ambiguous assertions to evidence-based comparisons with 
literature-based percentage differences. 
The significance of parameter sensitivity was further emphasized by supervisor 
input, especially with regard to discount rates (4 – 7%) and energy price escalation 
(2 – 5%). In response, I stated clearly the assumptions of my study (40 year 
lifespan, 5% discount rate, 3% energy escalation) and suggested sensitivity 
analysis as a primary goal. This improved the rigor and transparency of my study 
and immediately addressed the criticism that LCC outcomes can vary greatly in the 
absence of consistent assumptions.

(b) Difficulties Faced and Actions Taken to Overcome Them: 
The absence of localized cost data for sustainable buildings in Sydney was a 
significant obstacle. The majority of previous research employed national or 
international averages, which made it challenging to directly apply to Sydney's 
particular building cost structure (6 – 10% yearly growth). 
 Action: I highlighted this as a research gap in my paper and cited recent 
Australian studies, such as Infrastructure Australia's (2024) market capacity 
reports and ABS's (2024) construction price insights. 
 Result: This strengthened the industrial relevance of my research for NSW 
and Sydney in particular while enabling me to accept the restriction. 
Reconciling contradicting research on overall LCC savings was another challenge;

because of different discount rates.

energy prices (2 – 5%) impact overall LCC outcomes, I created a sensitivity 
analysis methodology.

IMPROVED LITERATURE REVIEW: 
Life Cycle Costing and Sustainable Construction 
An economic assessment technique called life cycle costing (LCC) is used to determine how 
much a structure will cost overall over the lifetime, including the expenses associated with initial 
construction, operation, maintenance, replacement, and disposal. According to research, 
operational costs make up between 60 and 80 percent of all building life cycle costs, making 
operational effectiveness a crucial component of long term economic performance. 
Sustainable buildings are made to use less energy and water while reducing their negative effects 
on the environment. Several studies have shown significant long-term operational savings, 
despite the fact that sustainable buildings typically require 5–15% greater initial construction 
costs than conventional buildings. Green buildings can cut energy use by about 25–30%, 
according to research by Zuo and Zhao (2017), while sustainable buildings can cut greenhouse 
gas emissions by up to 50%, according to GBCA data.
title: Project_Proposal_EPP

text:
according to research by Zuo and Zhao (2017), while sustainable buildings can cut greenhouse 
gas emissions by up to 50%, according to GBCA data. 
According to research by Cabeza et al. (2014), using LCC techniques increases decision-making 
accuracy in building projects by over 15% to 20%.  
Additionally, sustainable structures accomplish: 
 20 – 40% reduction in energy usage 
 30 – 50% reduction in water use 
 10 – 25% reduction in maintenance expenses 
Over the course of a building's 30–50 year lifespan, these reductions can lead to a 10–20% 
reduction in total life cycle expenses. 
Cost Optimization and Industry Importance 
Long-term cost planning is becoming more crucial since the Australian construction sector has 
seen yearly cost rises of between 6–10%. Sustainable design strategies assist environmental 
goals while lowering operating costs. Over 75% of newly built homes in New South Wales now 
meet 7-star energy efficiency criteria, indicating a growing trend in the use of sustainable 
building techniques. 
Important financial factors influencing LCC results include:

Research Gap: 
There is limited study of Sydney specific data in existing research, which mostly concentrate on 
worldwide or generic Australian data. Few studies combine sustainable performance metrics 
with realistic Quantity Surveying (QS) cost data. Furthermore, there is ambiguity when 
comparing the performance of conventional and sustainable buildings due to varying 
assumptions about energy escalation and discount rates. 
By performing a comparative LCC assessment with a particular focus on Sydney construction 
conditions and using consistent financial assumptions for analysis, this study seeks to overcome 
these constraints.able Questions: 
Primary Research Question: 
In terms of life cycle cost performance in Sydney construction and operating conditions, how do 
sustainable and conventional buildings compare? 
Sub Questions: 
a) In comparison to conventional structures, how much do sustainable buildings save 
operating costs? 
b) What effects do rising energy prices and discount rates have on life cycle costing results?

 Throughout the entire study process, academic integrity shall be upheld. 
 Calculations and financial data will be openly recorded.

Environmental Sustainability: 
By calculating the financial advantages of green buildings, this study advances sustainability 
objectives. Buildings consume over 40% of the world's energy; proving cost-effectiveness can 
hasten the adoption of sustainable design and help reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 30–50% 
(GBCA, 2023). 
Indigenous Knowledge and Sustainability: 
Based on in-depth ecological knowledge, Indigenous Australians have long engaged in 
sustainable land and resource management. Indigenous environmental stewardship values are 
respected in this study by:

change benefit from government sustainability goals (such as emissions reductions). 
No Indigenous cultural knowledge or materials are directly used in this secondary-data study.

There is no actual laboratory work involved. There is little risk to safety because all work is done
